<store>
Name: Fernhill Coffee Supply
Sells: Fernhill Coffee Supply sells home coffee brewing equipment and coffee beans. The range covers pour-over gear (ceramic and stainless steel drippers, size 02 paper filters, stovetop and electric gooseneck kettles, and a brew scale with timer), immersion brewers such as a French press and a cold brew jar, and manual and electric burr grinders. It also sells single-origin coffee beans from Fernhill Roastery in 250 g and 1 kg bags, whole bean or ground.
Audience: People who brew coffee at home, especially by pour-over or immersion, and who want to grind, weigh and control water temperature themselves. Some products, such as the single-dose flat-burr grinder and the temperature-hold kettle, suit buyers who care about precise brewing.
Tone: expert
Never say: —
</store>

content.text: {"title":"How to Use a French Press: A Step-by-Step Guide to a Clean, Full-Bodied Cup","angle":"The reader will know the ratio, grind, water temperature, steep time and plunge-and-pour technique that make French press coffee full-bodied without sludge, plus how to keep the press clean.","sections":[{"heading":"Why the French press tastes the way it does","covers":"How immersion brewing works: the grounds steep fully in the water, then a metal mesh filter separates them, letting oils and fine particles through for a heavier body than paper-filtered pour-over. Introduces the Fernhill French Press and its build.","facts":["F2","F4","F5","F7"]},{"heading":"What you need: ratio, dose and batch size","covers":"A starting ratio of about 1:15 to 1:16 (around 60–65 g coffee per litre of water), scaling down for smaller batches, and weighing coffee and water rather than using scoops. How much the 1-litre press makes.","facts":["F1","F6"]},{"heading":"Grind coarse and grind fresh","covers":"Why a coarse, even grind matters: it slows extraction and leaves fewer fines to slip through the mesh and muddy the cup. Grinding just before brewing, and using a burr grinder with a dedicated coarse setting. Multiple fills of a small hopper for a full litre.","facts":["F10","F12","F13","F14","F15"]},{"heading":"Step by step: brewing your French press","covers":"Preheat the beaker; add the grounds; pour water just off the boil (roughly 93–96 °C); stir or bloom; steep about 4 minutes; break the crust and skim the foam and floating grounds for a cleaner cup; optionally wait a few minutes more for fines to settle; plunge slowly and gently; pour all of it out straight away so it does not keep extracting.","facts":["F2","F7"]},{"heading":"Choosing beans for the French press","covers":"Medium roasts with chocolate and caramel notes suit the heavy body of immersion; a washed coffee gives a clean, sweet base. How to adjust grind and steep time if the cup tastes sour (finer or longer) or bitter (coarser or shorter).","facts":["F19","F22","F28","F30"]},{"heading":"Cleaning and care","covers":"Disposing of grounds (not down the sink), rinsing the mesh after every brew, and fully disassembling the plunger and filter regularly to remove trapped oils that turn rancid. What to do if the glass beaker breaks.","facts":["F8","F9","F4"]},{"heading":"Beyond hot brew: cold brew by immersion","covers":"A brief note that the same immersion principle works cold, with a long fridge steep, and when a dedicated cold brew jar is more convenient than a French press.","facts":["F43","F48","F51"]}],"products":["P1","P2","P3"],"links":["P1","P2","P3","P5","L2","L3","L4"]}
